rows.reason: Six sentences; the house form allows 3-5. Content is accurate (lines 1-2: 'sat down on / a stile which led thence into a field'), but the script must lose a sentence.
'attested by' is on line 3 and the sheet of ice covering the causeway on line 4; rules out option A with 'did not feel the cold'.
'as the path was narrow, I sat / still' is on lines 10-11; script points to 'narrow' and rules out 'just leaving the stile'.
'Man and horse were down; they had slipped on' (line 28) runs into 'the sheet of ice which glazed the causeway' (line 29); the ice is also on line 4.
Line 49 speech 'I have no broken bones,-only a sprain' gives what he has not and has; line 50 'tried his foot' and 'Ugh!' is correct.
Line 1 to the first comma, 'As Canterville Chase is seven miles from Ascot, the nearest railway station,' gives the reason before the telegraphing; line 3 is the evening scene.
Squirrels 'peered at them from the beech-trees' (line 6) and rabbits 'scudded away... with their white tails in the air' (lines 6-7); key named after the evidence.

Never reaches the key. It says 'One made a request; another agreed to it. Read which way round it goes.' but never shows that line 14 gives 'at Lady Canterville's earnest request' and Mrs Otis 'had consented', so the child is not told which way round it goes, and that is the step that rules out the reversal distractor.
'tea laid out for them' (line 18), 'after taking off their wraps, they sat down' (line 19), 'fine Tudor hall' (line 17) are all on the lines cited.

'She says what she is afraid of' takes the polite idiom 'I am afraid something has been spilt' as fear, which misleads. The last sentence, 'What Mrs Umney says next is not yet hers.', is opaque to a 9-11-year-old: it does not say what Mrs Umney says or why that rules out option B.
Plumcakes, jellies (line 2) and gravy (line 3) are the scents; line 3 'impossible to feel altogether gloomy' answers the question. The visitors are ruled out correctly.
Question 'shall you run away to-morrow?' (line 8), answer 'no, I sha'n't' (line 10), 'eying the third' puff (line 9) are all on the lines cited.

Never shows the answer words. The script cites lines 16 and 18, then says only 'Then he names what it really is.' It does not point to 'It's the pudden' (line 18) or 'apricot roll-up' (line 19), and it does not connect 'pudden' to the key's 'pudding'. The closing sentence about the exclamation answers a question nobody asked.
'right hand or left?' (line 27), 'Right or left,-you choose' (line 30), 'keep your eyes shut' (line 31) and Maggie's reply on line 28 are all correctly placed.
'Tom had finished first, and had to / look on' (lines 43-44) and 'a capacity for more' (line 44) are correct, and lines 45-46 are correctly put down to Maggie.

'Line 2 gives the reason he turned round' claims something the passage does not say, because Jim never turns round. It also skips the question's own anchor, 'I ran on deck.' on line 2, which is the sentence the apple explains.
Line 6 'In I got bodily into the apple barrel, and found there was scarce an apple left' is correct, and the heavy man sits down at line 9.
'I didn't half a quarter like the job till I' (line 27), 'had this talk with you, John; but there's my hand on it now' (line 28) show he is won over.
Line 41 'I've had a'most enough o' Cap'n Smollett; he's hazed me long enough' gives the reason; pickles and wines are on line 42.
Lines 1-2 'He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied'. The jeering on line 3 is correctly called something he pictures ahead.
'Ben's gait was the hop-skip-and-jump' (lines 11-12) is 'proof enough that his heart was light' (line 12). The script correctly separates the sign from what it proves.
'paid no attention' (line 15) and 'Tom's mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work' (line 19) are correct.
'it wouldn't hardly do' (line 40), 'awful particular about this fence' (lines 40-41 and 42), and 'one boy in a thousand' (line 43) are correct. The first 'this fence' runs on to line 41.
'nothing at all particular about the knocker' (line 1) 'except that it was very large' (line 2) is correct, and 'seen it, night and morning' is on lines 2-3.
'had not bestowed one thought on Marley' (line 6) 'since his last mention... that afternoon' (lines 6-7) is correct, and the key in the lock is on line 8.
'put his / hand upon the key he had relinquished, turned it sturdily, walked in' (lines 20-21) is correct, and the candle comes after (lines 21-22).
'the dying flame leaped up' (line 69) 'and fell again' (line 70) is correct, and the words in between are correctly called what the leap seemed to say.
'there is your first sight of the moor' (line 1) and 'pointing out of the carriage window' (line 2) are correct, and the fields and wood are on line 3.

'Line 18 says that behind the peaceful and sunlit countryside there rose ever something.' The words 'there rose ever' are on line 19, not line 18. 'rose ever something' is also not English a 9-11-year-old reads easily.
Heath-clad land (line 31), 'a mounted / soldier' on the summit with 'rifle poised' (lines 32-33), and 'watching the / road' (lines 33-34) are correct.

'Line 59 gives the old stone pillars on either side.' The passage never says the pillars are stone. Line 59 has 'weather-bitten pillars on either side, blotched with lichens'. That matters here because a distractor is 'A stone lamp'.
'sported a bit of literature' (line 3) and 'any numbers of The Pickwick Papers' (line 4, 'publishing in parts' line 5) are correct, and the trays and cards are on lines 1-2.

Never points to 'considered herself literary' (lines 7-8), the words the question asks about. It ties the sermons to 'took any talk of books as a challenge' instead. It also names the rector (distractor A) without ruling it out, and 'the strength she went on' is not easy English for a child.
'The same line says he had it only that morning.' Line 20 ends 'I had it'. The words 'only this morning' are on line 21, so the citation is wrong.
'How was the Rambler published' asked 'in a low voice' (line 36) and 'Miss Jenkyns could not have heard' (line 37) are correct.

'Dr Johnson's style is a model for young beginners' (line 38) and 'I recommend it to / your favourite' (lines 39-40), where the favourite is Mr Boz (line 29), are correct, and her letters are rightly called the example.
'favoring the horses' (line 3) 'yet never losing sight of the fact that he carried the mail' (lines 3-4) is correct.
'she nodded to a / child who was eagerly waiting... ran towards her as if she feared / to be a moment too late' (lines 10-12) is correct, and 'small for her age' is on line 13.
'a small voice above the rattle and rumble of the wheels' (line 36) and 'At first he thought it was a cricket, a tree toad, or a bird' (line 37) are correct, and the shape comes at line 39.
'there ain't no extry charge to sit side o' me' (line 50) gives the cost, and 'boosted her up to the front seat' (line 51) is rightly called what she gets.
'smoothing her dress under her' (line 53) and 'putting her sunshade under its extended folds between the driver and herself' (line 54) are correct, and 'pushed back her hat' is on line 55.
